subject: Culture
title: Turning of the Bones
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: Turning of the Bones.

hook.text: In Madagascar, families dig up their dead, wrap them in fresh cloth, and dance with the corpses in a joyful reunion.

buildup.text: The ritual, called 'famadihana,' happens every five to seven years. It's the most important social event in the area.

discovery.text: The Malagasy believe the dead are not truly gone until everyone who remembers them has also died.

twist.text: The ceremony costs months of savings. Families go into debt because honoring ancestors is worth more than comfort.

climax.text: Health officials worry about disease exposure. But banning the ritual would sever the community's deepest bond.

punchline.text: Some bonds don't end at the grave—they visit it.

quiz.question: How often is 'famadihana' performed in Madagascar?

details.summary: In Madagascar's famadihana ceremony, families exhume their dead every five to seven years, rewrap them in fresh silk shrouds, dance with the bodies, and share family news with the deceased. This 'turning of the bones' maintains an ongoing relationship between the living and dead.
details.whyItMatters: Famadihana challenges the Western notion that death ends the relationship. It shows that for many cultures, the dead remain active family members requiring care and connection.
takeaways: Famadihana involves exhuming and rewrapping deceased family members
Families dance with the wrapped bodies and share news
The ceremony reinforces family bonds across the boundary of death

faq.question: How does famadihana work?
faq.answer: Every five to seven years, families open the family tomb, remove the wrapped bodies, and replace the old silk shrouds (lambamena) with fresh ones. They hold the bodies above their heads and dance around the tomb while a band plays.

faq.question: Is famadihana still practiced?
faq.answer: Yes, though it faces pressure from Christian missionaries, health authorities concerned about plague transmission, and the cost of new silk shrouds. Younger Malagasy increasingly question the practice, but many families continue it as an essential cultural and spiritual obligation.
